schools.summary: Gill catalogues the weariness by what it is not — not Cain's guilty horror nor Paul's holy longing — but a man whose body is one sore, uneasy to dwell longer in the earthly tabernacle.

Clarke reads nephesh as the immortal soul, not the animal life (chai), proof Job was no materialist, and takes 'leave my complaint upon myself' as self-blame; Wesley hears the opening 'Shall I give over complaining?'
Ellicott reads 'I will leave my complaint' as 'I will give free vent to the complaint that is upon me' (cf. Job 9:27), against the self-blame reading.

Henry: daunted by God's majesty, Job vents not by violent hands but violent words, speaking the bitterness of his soul, not his settled judgment, and leaving the blame on himself rather than impeaching God.

debates.question: Does 'I will leave my complaint upon myself' mean self-blame or free vent?

sides.position: charge the cause upon myself, and not impeach my Maker
give free vent to the complaint that is upon me

themes: the soul not the animal life
bitterness of soul, not settled judgment

schools.summary: Gill: 'condemn me' cannot mean eternal condemnation (none to those in Christ) but 'account me not wicked' — God knew Job was not the man his friends supposed.

Keil renders 'Condemn me not; let me know wherefore Thou contendest,' the cry of one begging not to die the death of the wicked against his conscience; Ellicott calls it a model of prayer joining the publican's cry (Luke 18:13) with a longing for light.
Clarke: 'let me not be afflicted in thy wrath'; God afflicts only for past sin, to try, or to manifest grace, so let the sin be named; Wesley: 'discover my integrity by removing this stroke.'
Gill calls the expostulation too bold and free, yet grants the premise: God dehorts men from oppression and helps the oppressed, so takes no pleasure in it; Job errs in thinking his affliction such.

Clarke unfolds the clauses: it can be no gratification to distress God's own handiwork, and Job's suffering seems to 'shine upon' the wicked's verdict that religion profits nothing; Wesley: 'Far be it from Job to think God did him wrong,' only at a loss to reconcile providence with justice.

themes: despising the work of thy hands
shining on the counsel of the wicked

schools.summary: God has eyes of mercy and of displeasure but not fleshly ones; unlike man's eyes, his see all at once, pierce the dark, and read the heart.
Clarke sums the verse: 'Dost thou judge as man judges?'
Keil sets the question at the head of the passage on man's making, the embryo's forming reckoned by the Hebrew wisdom one of the deepest mysteries (cf. Eccl. 11:5).
Henry: God, being Spirit, judges not as men who go by what is alleged and proved and the bias of interest, but according to truth, trying the heart by his own inspection.

themes: God sees not as man sees

schools.summary: Not so few (a thousand years as one day) nor so changeable; the dispensations change but the divine nature and purpose do not.

Clarke distinguishes enosh (wretched man) from gaber (the strong man), neither to be measured against God; Wesley: a mortal judge must hurry lest death rob him of justice, but the eternal God, seeing all at one view, needs no long scrutiny.
Keil reads the couplet to the same force: God is not short-lived like man, to whom truth is the daughter of time.
Henry: men grow wiser only by slow experience; to God nothing is past or future but all present.

themes: are thy days as the days of man?

schools.summary: Gill: God narrowly audits every action as if there were no Mediator or forgiveness, the affliction meant to rack a confession out of him.
Clarke: 'Is it becoming thy infinite dignity to concern thyself with the transgressions of a despicable mortal?'; Wesley: 'keeping me so long upon the rack, to compel me to accuse myself.'
Henry: the prolonged inquest wears an aspect dishonourable to God; Job pleads God's own honour — 'do something for thy great name' (Jer. 14:21).
Job does not claim sinlessness (he owns himself a sinner) but denies he is the wicked hypocrite his friends read in his suffering, appealing to the Searcher of hearts.
Clarke: why sift me as if to find sin when none can be found?; Wesley: 'wicked' = hypocrite as friends account me, yet none can deliver from God's hand, so I submit to his sovereign will.
Ellicott: the sense is rather 'that I shall not be found guilty' — the language the Psalmist borrows in Ps. 119:73, not Peter's appeal (John 21:17).
Henry finds the comfort: it is vain to contend with Omnipotence, but sweet to say 'thou knowest I am not wicked, for thou knowest I love thee.'

debates.question: Is 'I am not wicked' a claim of present innocence or a forensic 'I shall not be found guilty'?

sides.position: a protest of integrity — not the wicked hypocrite his friends suppose
a forensic future — 'that I shall not be found guilty'

themes: thou knowest I am not wicked
none can deliver out of thine hand

schools.summary: The whole plea is meant to move God to pity: God alone (not Job's parents) made him a curious piece; Gill checks pressing 'hands' into a distinct reference to the Son and Spirit.

Clarke lingers on the craftsmanship — the harmony (yachad) and completion (sabib) of the parts — against the terrible verb 'thou wilt swallow me up'; how dreadful an evil sin must be, to dissolve such work to dust.
Keil renders 'Thy hands have formed and perfected me altogether round about, and Thou hast now swallowed me up!'
Henry makes it the plea of the clay to the potter (Isa. 64:8; Ps. 119:73): thou madest me by an act of sovereignty; wilt thou unmake me? and thou knowest me, so needest not examine me by scourging.
Man is 'as the clay' not for impurity (God made him upright) but for brittleness — a frail vessel needing no heavy stroke to break it.

Clarke: fashioned with such skill men suppose a permanent being, 'but thou hast decreed to turn them into dust'; Wesley finds two pleas — the frailty of the clay and the excellency of the artifice from mean materials.
Ellicott ties the return to dust to Ps. 22:15; Keil keeps the plea that the God who made him as clay remember it before crumbling him.
Henry turns 'remember' into the saint's prayer: 'thou hast made me; do thou new-make me; I am thine, save me.'

themes: wilt thou bring me into dust again?

schools.summary: Gill takes the milk as the modest figure of conception from the parents' seed, likened to milk for being liquid and for its colour.

Clarke argues strongly for generation/the embryo over mere nutrition, the pouring, curdling, clothing, and fencing 'well imagined'; Wesley: God makes man from a small, milky substance by degrees congealed into an exquisite frame.
Ellicott calls it 'an allusion to the embryo' (cf. Ps. 139:13).
Henry: the elegant simile of the body formed in the womb, milk coagulated into cheese.

debates.question: Do the milk-and-curd images describe embryonic generation or bodily nutrition?

sides.position: the forming of the embryo / generation

schools.summary: Two garments — bones clothed with flesh within, flesh with skin without, a covering of arteries, nerves, and pores of exquisite fineness; the inward parts formed first, then the outward for defence.
Wesley: God covered the inward, nobler parts first; the bones the stay and strength, skull and ribs enclosing the vital organs.

Henry: skin and flesh the body's clothing, bones and sinews its defensive armour — an illustrious instance of the Creator's wisdom, a pity such bodies serve unrighteousness when fit to be temples of the Holy Ghost.
Keil keeps the plain rendering, the anatomy speaking for itself as one more clause in the argument from creation.
'Life and favour' — natural life quickened in the womb, and also the spiritual life given when one dead in trespasses is quickened by the Spirit of life from Christ.

Clarke: God's continual visitation preserves life, for 'in him we live, move, and have our being' (Acts 17:28); Wesley: life given and maintained, with nourishment, education, and knowledge — 'wilt thou now undo all that thou hast done?'
Henry: life is a favour, more than meat, a distinguishing favour; God lights the lamp of life and feeds it with fresh oil, his visitation preserving the spirit.
Keil renders 'Life and favour Thou hast shown me, and thy care hath guarded my breath.'

themes: the visitation that preserves the spirit

schools.summary: Gill inclines to the darker sense: 'these things' are the afflictions God decreed and stored up, held in reserve even while he formed and favoured Job.
Ellicott: Job's sense of God's goodness is embittered by the thought that God kept these sorrows in reserve, meaning eventually to overwhelm him; Keil renders 'I perceive that this was in Thy mind.'
Clarke hears hidden gracious purposes and proofs of kindness; Wesley takes it of both former favours and present frowns, according to one consistent will.
Henry: God's changing dealings spring from one settled purpose, dark now but consistent — 'we are bound to believe there are good reasons hidden in his heart.'

debates.question: What has God 'hid in his heart' — mercy or coming judgment?

sides.position: the afflictions purposed and held in reserve
gracious purposes and kindness not yet made known
both favours and frowns, of one consistent will

themes: hidden in the heart of God
faith owning what it cannot explain

schools.summary: 'Markest me' — God takes strict notice of his sins and lays them up, or shuts him in a prison of affliction; even his sacrifice for sin (Gussetius) is not regarded.
Clarke: nothing can be hidden from God, who takes account of the transgression and cannot hold the guilty innocent.
Henry hears a charge of summum jus — every false step marked by conscience God's deputy — yet answers that God does not in fact deal with his own in extremity.

Keil reads the hypothetical suppositions (if I sin, if I be wicked, if I be righteous) as a man boxed in; Ellicott renders the whole as one conditional — sin marked, guilt woe, righteousness not daring to lift its head.

themes: if I sin, thou markest me

schools.summary: 'If I be wicked, woe is me' — afflictions here and everlasting wrath hereafter, or the Targum's 'destruction from the great judgment.'
Clarke balances the equation — wicked, he meets punishment; righteous, he can claim no favour — so 'full of confusion'; Wesley: whether hypocrite or upright, 'all comes to one,' with no comfort.
Henry: a sinful state is woeful, yet even the righteous Job dares not lift up his head, full of confusion of face and spirit (Ps. 88:15), praying God to 'see' his affliction (Ps. 25:18).
Keil and Ellicott read the movement into a plea; Ellicott paraphrases 'I am full of shame; therefore behold Thou mine affliction, for only by Thy taking note of it can I find relief.'

themes: woe if wicked, no lifting the head if righteous
guilt and innocence at one dead end

schools.summary: 'It increaseth' of the affliction growing, or a wish that it would reach its height and end him; the proud waves lifting to overwhelm.

Clarke reads the lion as Job hunted by his friends and God's works past finding out; Wesley makes God the lion who, unlike a beast that ends its prey's torment, renews the calamities and makes the plagues marvellous for kind, extremity, and continuance.
Keil makes God himself the lion and Job the prey (cf. Hos. 5:14); Ellicott owns the verse very obscure, offering three constructions of its subject — the hunting, the lifted head, or the affliction.
Henry: God showed himself marvellous upon Job, making him a prodigy and a wonder, the affliction most grievous because he felt God's indignation in it.

debates.question: Who is the hunting lion, and who the prey?

sides.position: God the lion, Job the hunted prey
Job the king of beasts, hunted by his friends

outliers.note: Reads the fierce lion as Job himself, the king of beasts, hunted not by God but by his friends who 'attack me on every side.'

schools.summary: The renewed 'witnesses' are afflictions repeated daily, or the strokes his friends and the world read as proofs of his wickedness — not devils or the friends themselves.

Clarke: the terms are forensic, witnesses in continual succession, and 'changes and war' fresh troops relieving one another; Wesley: the witnesses are God's judgments, evidences of sin and wrath, the army their great number.

Ellicott judges the figure forensic (relays, a host, the ministers of God's vengeance) rather than the sores his friends took as proofs, and marvels at the sublimity and awe of so daring an indictment standing in Holy Writ; Keil keeps it the hinge into the longing for death.

sides.position: the afflictions and judgments themselves, brought as evidence
fresh forensic witnesses, a summoned host, the ministers of God's vengeance
the sores on Job's body, which the friends read as proofs of guilt

themes: the awe of Job's words in Scripture

schools.summary: God rightly the author of the bringing-forth; unmoved by his friends, Job holds and repeats the mind in which he cursed his birth.
Clarke: 'Why give me being, when thou didst foresee I should be exposed to such hardships?' — reverting to the curse of chapter 3.
Ellicott: Job reverts to the strain of his original curse (Job 3:11); Keil reads the clauses as conditionals of the death that never came.

Henry calls it a relapse of passion — life called a favour in v.12, now a burden — yet passes on Caryl's charitable turn, that Job grieved to be hindered from glorifying God, though we may glorify him in the fires.

outliers.note: Passes on Caryl's charitable reading that Job's wish to have died sprang from grief at being hindered, as he thought, from the great end of glorifying God — his harp hung on the willows — though grounded on the mistake that God cannot be glorified in the fires.

themes: life a favour turned a burden

schools.summary: 'As though I had not been' means not utter non-existence but a life comparatively forgotten — unseen, unnamed, buried at once in oblivion — which Job wishes for himself.
Clarke: had he died at birth, unconscious of existence, it would be 'as though I had never been,' carried straight from womb to grave without the interval of suffering.
Keil joins the verse tightly to the plea for respite that follows.
Henry draws a counsel for the living: not to be over-fond of life, nor over-lament infants carried from womb to grave, whose lot we ourselves may sometimes wish.

themes: as though I had not been
carried from the womb to the grave

schools.summary: The days of every man are few, Job's fewer, no more than a handbreadth before God — the brevity itself a plea for respite.
Wesley: 'My life is short and hastens to an end; there is no need thou shouldest grudge me some ease for so small a moment.'

Ellicott notes the variant 'Let him cease' and owns the reply 'moves upon the very verge of blasphemy,' redeemed only by its pervading reverence — Job, like Jacob, wrestling with God in the dark, yet never giving up faith.
Henry reads a tender prayer for intermission, the plea 'are not my days few?' fastening on the goodness of God's nature, and turning back on us to redeem the time.

outliers.note: Judges the reply to move 'upon the very verge of blasphemy,' redeemed only by its pervading reverence and undertone of faith — Job wrestling with God like Jacob in the dark, an unburdening God is not displeased with.

themes: a plea for a little respite
on the verge of blasphemy yet reverent

schools.summary: 'Whence I shall not return' of no return to this life and its affairs, not a denial of the resurrection, which Job elsewhere strongly asserts.
Clarke hears in the heaped, obscure terms a confession of our ignorance of the state of separate spirits; the land of darkness a place where death rules and projects his shadow.
Keil keeps the couplet as the threshold of the closing description of the grave.
Henry: 'give me some ease before I die' (Ps. 13:3); the grave a fixed and, to nature, melancholy state, which only extreme misery could make Job wish for.

themes: not a denial of the resurrection

schools.summary: Not merely like darkness but darkness itself — gross thick darkness like Egypt's, that might be felt, the very blackness of darkness.
Clarke on 'light as darkness' — a palpable obscure (Sophocles' 'thou darkness be my light,' the Vulgate's 'no order but sempiternal horror'); a duration out of time, on the confines of eternity.
Keil renders a land of deep darkness like midnight, of the shadow of death and confusion, 'bright like midnight.'
Henry reads the disorder and darkness as the negatives of mercy — no order, no light, no knowledge or praise — yet dark to man, the grave is not dark to God, whose eye keeps the dust of the saints.

themes: a land of darkness as darkness itself
where the light is as darkness
